'''''Sonchus oleraceus''''' is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the tribe [[Cichorieae]] of the family [[Asteraceae]], [[native species|native]] to Europe and Western Asia. It has many [[common name]]s including '''common sowthistle''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SOOL|taxon=Sonchus oleraceus|accessdate=19 November 2015}}</ref> '''sow thistle''',<ref>[http://www.pfaf.org/database/plants.php?Sonchus+oleraceus ''Sonchus oleraceus''] at [[Plants For A Future]]</ref> '''smooth sow thistle''', '''annual sow thistle''', '''puha''' (in [[New Zealand English]], from [[Māori language|Māori]] {{Lang|mi|pūhā}}),<ref name=TMR/><ref>{{Cite web |title=Puha |publisher= Herb Federation of New Zealand |url= https://herbs.org.nz/herbs/puha/ |access-date=5 September 2026}}</ref> '''hare's colwort''', '''hare's thistle''', '''milky tassel''', '''milk thistle''',<ref name="eiwf">{{cite web |title= Sonchus oleraceus |publisher= International Environmental Weed Foundation |url= https://www.iewf.org/weedid/Sonchus_oleraceus.htm |access-date=3 September 2026}}</ref> and '''soft thistle'''.<ref name=eiwf/>

== Description ==
This [[annual plant]] has a hollow, upright stem up to {{convert|30 to 100|cm}} high.<ref>{{ cite book | first1=Yoshitaka | last1=Tanaka | first2=Nguyen | last2=Van Ke | date=2007 | title=Edible Wild Plants of Vietnam: The Bountiful Garden | publisher=Thailand: Orchid Press | isbn=978-9745240896 | page=52}}</ref> It prefers full sun, and can tolerate most soil conditions. The flowers are [[hermaphroditic flower|hermaphroditic]], and common pollinators include bees and flies.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.pfaf.org/database/plants.php?Sonchus+oleraceus|title = Sonchus oleraceus Sow Thistle, Common sowthistle PFAF Plant Database}}</ref> It spreads by seeds being carried by wind or water.

== Etymology ==
Its [[Binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] {{wikt-lang|la|holeraceus|oleraceus}} means "vegetable/herbal".<ref>{{cite book |last=Parker |first=Peter |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=O-tzDQAAQBAJ&pg=PT328 |title=A Little Book of Latin for Gardeners |date=2018 |publisher=Little Brown Book Group |isbn=978-1-4087-0615-2 |page=328 |quote={{lang|la|oleraceus, holeraceus}} = relating to vegetables or kitchen garden}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Whitney |first=William Dwight |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OGTWRtstsaEC&pg=PA2856 |title=The Century Dictionary and Cyclopedia |publisher=Century Co. |year=1899 |page=2856 |quote={{abbr|L.|Latin}} {{lang|la|holeraceus}}, {{abbr|prop.|properly}} {{lang|la|oleraceus}}, herb-like, {{lang|la|holus}}, {{abbr|prop.|properly}} {{lang|la|olus}} ({{lang|la|oler-}}), herbs, vegetables}}</ref>{{Efn|For the [[generic name (biology)|generic name]]'s etymology, see ''[[Sonchus]]''.}} The common name 'sow thistle' refers to its attractiveness to pigs, and the similarity of the leaf to younger [[thistle]] plants. The common name 'hare's thistle' refers to its purported beneficial effects on hare and rabbits.<ref name="Grieve">{{cite web |title=A Modern Herbal | Sow-Thistles |url=http://www.botanical.com/botanical/mgmh/s/sowthi71.html |access-date=2014-07-12 |publisher=Botanical.com}}</ref>

== Invasiveness ==
Annual sowthistle is considered an [[invasive species]] due to its rapid growth, prolific seed production, and wide dispersal. The plant thrives in disturbed environments, such as roadsides and agricultural fields, spreading aggressively through [[Biological dispersal|wind-dispersed]] seeds. It forms dense populations that outcompete [[native vegetation]] by quickly establishing in open areas, particularly after soil disturbance. Sowthistle's resilience to various soil types and its ability to reseed itself make it difficult to control in many regions.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sonchus (Common Sowthistle, Hare's Thistle, Milky Tassel, Sowthistle, Sow Thistle) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/sonchus/ |access-date=2024-09-11 |website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref><ref>[http://plants.ifas.ufl.edu/sonole.html ''Sonchus oleraceus''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070428180750/http://plants.ifas.ufl.edu/sonole.html |date=2007-04-28 }} at [http://plants.ifas.ufl.edu/welcome.html Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070325214633/http://plants.ifas.ufl.edu/welcome.html |date=2007-03-25 }}</ref><ref name="pier">[http://www.hear.org/pier/species/sonchus_oleraceus.htm Sonchus oleraceus L., Asteraceae], Pacific Island Ecosystems at Risk (PIER)</ref> 

In Australia it is a common and widespread invasive species, with large infestations a serious problem in crops.<ref>{{cite web|title=Common sowthistle ''Sonchus oleraceus'' |url=http://www.weeds.org.au/cgi-bin/weedident.cgi?tpl=plant.tpl&state=&s=&ibra=all&card=H73|website=Weeds Australia|access-date=25 September 2014}}</ref>

==Uses==
[[File:Amanida de lletsons9.JPG|thumb|Green salad with [[carrot]], [[cucumber]], [[onion]], sowthistle leaves, and tomato slices]]

The leaves are eaten as salad greens or cooked like spinach. This is one of the species used in [[Chinese cuisine]] as ''kŭcài'' ([[wikt:苦菜|苦菜]]; lit. bitter vegetable).{{Citation needed|date=October 2020}} The younger leaves are less bitter and better to eat raw. Steaming can remove the bitterness of older leaves.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Nyerges |first1=Christopher |title=Foraging Wild Edible Plants of North America: More than 150 Delicious Recipes Using Nature's Edibles |date=2016 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |isbn=978-1-4930-1499-6 |page=169 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RwDHCgAAQBAJ}}</ref> The younger roots are also edible and can suffice as a [[coffee substitute]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Nyerges|first=Christopher|title=Foraging Washington: Finding, Identifying, and Preparing Edible Wild Foods|publisher=Falcon Guides|year=2017|isbn=978-1-4930-2534-3|location=Guilford, CT|oclc=965922681}}</ref>

=== Herbalism ===
''Sonchus oleraceus'' has a variety of uses in [[herbalism]]. It also has been ascribed [[medicine|medicinal]] qualities similar to [[dandelion]] and [[succory]].<ref name=Grieve/> When the plant was introduced to [[New Zealand]], the [[Māori people]] found it similar to and as palatable as their native {{Lang|mi|pūhā}} or [[Sonchus kirkii|''S. kirkii'']] (also known as ''raurōroa''),<ref name="TMR">{{cite web |title=Proto-Polynesian Etymologies: *Pūfā ~ Pūhā, Pūwhā |url=https://www.temarareo.org/PPN-Pufa.html |website=Te Māra Reo |publisher=Benton Family Trust |access-date=26 February 2025}}</ref> thus also picked up ''S. oleraceus'' (since also named ''rauriki'') for similar food and medical use.<ref name="CambieFerguson2003">{{cite journal|last1=Cambie|first1=Richard C|last2=Ferguson|first2=Lynnette R|title=Potential functional foods in the traditional Maori diet|journal=Mutation Research/Fundamental and Molecular Mechanisms of Mutagenesis|volume=523-524|year=2003|pages=109–117|issn=0027-5107|doi=10.1016/S0027-5107(02)00344-5|pmid=12628508}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | title=Puha • Herb Federation of New Zealand | url=https://herbs.org.nz/herbs/puha/ | access-date=2025-08-04 | website=herbs.org.nz}}</ref>

Native Americans had many uses for this plant. [[Pima people|Pima]] used its gum as a "cure for the opium habit", as a cathartic, and as a food, where the "leaves and stems [were] rubbed between the palms of the hands and eaten raw" and sometimes "boiled". The [[Yaqui]] used the plant as a vegetable, where the "tender, young leaves [were] boiled in salted water with chile and eaten as greens." The Kamia ([[Kumeyaay]]) "boiled leaves for food as greens". The Houma used it as an [[abortifacient]] where an "infusion of [the] plant [was] taken to 'make tardy menstruation come;'" an antidiarrheal; for children that were teething; and as hog feed.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://naeb.brit.org/uses/species/3755/|title=BRIT - Native American Ethnobotany Database}}</ref>

The [[Samaritans]] eat the leafs of this bitter plant on the feast of passover. The bitter leafs are eaten together with [[Passover sacrifice|Paschal lamb]] and [[unleavened bread]], as dictated by the Bible (Exodus 12, 8): "They shall eat the flesh that night, roasted on the fire; with unleavened bread and bitter herbs they shall eat it." Thus, the Samaritans identify ''Sonchus oleraceus'' with the bitter herbs.
